entries.title: Dynamical Variational Theory of Stochastic Reaction Networks
entries.abstract: Discrete stochastic population dynamics describe systems ranging from biochemical reaction networks and gene regulation to epidemic spreading, ecology, and population genetics, where finite populations generate strong intrinsic fluctuations. Predicting their dynamics, including mean populations, fluctuations, time-lagged correlations, response functions, and steady states, remains challenging: the chemical master equation admits no general analytical solution, numerical solutions scale poorly with system size, and standard approximations fail at low copy numbers. Using a field-theoretic representation of the reaction dynamics, we develop a dynamical variational approximation for stochastic reaction networks based on the Plefka expansion from spin-glass physics. For reaction systems with general stoichiometry and time-dependent rates, the expansion yields tractable non-Markovian effective dynamics with self-consistent memory. We further introduce a generalized self-consistent bubble resummation that provides closed predictions for means, correlations, and response functions. The formulation applies broadly to discrete stochastic population dynamics on networks, and we provide a numerical implementation with adaptive time stepping for user-defined systems. We benchmark the method on stochastic gene regulation, enzyme kinetics, and infection dynamics, where it accurately captures both time-dependent behaviour and steady states, including fluctuation-driven effects missed by conventional approximations. Together, these results establish a general analytical framework for stochastic reaction dynamics across transient and stationary regimes in strongly fluctuating low-copy-number systems.

entries.title: From Sequence Uncertainty to Phenotype Hypotheses: Uncertainty-Conditioned Inference over Biomedical Knowledge Graphs
entries.abstract: Genomic foundation models provide variant-level evidence, but connecting that evidence to phenotype hypotheses requires accounting for uncertainty throughout structured reasoning. We introduce an uncertainty-conditioned path-energy framework that converts sequence predictions and calibrated predictive uncertainty into explicit distributions over graph-supported phenotype hypotheses, without patient-level phenotype supervision. An interpretable learned energy scores admissible gene--disease--phenotype routes, query uncertainty controls the target temperature, and path probabilities are aggregated into phenotype hypotheses. This formulation makes evidence quality an explicit determinant of hypothesis breadth while retaining traceable multi-path support. Exact normalization over enumerable candidate sets provides a reference for evaluating a Hastings-corrected learned revision operator. On AlzKB and Hetionet, phenotype-level entropy tracks upstream uncertainty, with Spearman correlations of 0.951 and 0.878, respectively; ablations identify the contribution of uncertainty conditioning. In masked-edge recovery, the model exceeds chance and degree-matched probability-permutation controls. Training the energy under the uncertainty-dependent temperature yields higher held-out recall@10 than training under a constant temperature of comparable magnitude. Under gene hold-out, recall@10 exceeds that of a trained DistMult embedding on 24 of 30 graph masks (0.183 versus 0.123); this difference is attributable mainly to three genes with many variants and is not established for all genes. These results establish an uncertainty-aware interface from genomic predictions to graph-supported phenotype hypotheses that combines interpretable probability allocation with held-out association recovery of explicitly stated scope.

entries.title: Towards consensus on practical probabilistic evaluation metrics for clinical decision making in radiotherapy
entries.abstract: Introduction: The main aim of this paper is to identify clinically feasible probabilistic evaluation approaches for radiotherapy and to assess whether they can support clinical decision making better than current robustness evaluation approaches. To this end, we calibrate probabilistic clinical goals and identify evaluation metrics with a team of medical physics experts and apply these to three patient cohorts. Methods: Sixty intensity-modulated proton therapy plans from three Dutch proton centers were included: 20 neuro-oncological, 20 head-and-neck, and 20 breast cancer cases. Probabilistic evaluation was performed using polynomial chaos expansion with 10,000 simulated fractionated treatments per case. Volumetric and dosimetric CTV goals were calibrated at a 90% probability level. Selected probabilistic evaluation metrics were applied to representative patient cases and eight radiation oncologists participated in semi-structured interviews addressing preferred metrics and probability levels. Results: The calibrated volumetric goals were V0.95Dpres = 99.95%, 99.80% and 99.54% at a 90% probability level for the neuro-oncological, head-and-neck, and breast cohorts, respectively. The dosimetric goals were D98%,CTV = 0.973Dpres, 0.968Dpres and 0.967Dpres at a 90% probability level. All radiation oncologists considered the probabilistic evaluation metrics suitable for clinical decision making, and most regarded them as an improvement over the currently used VWmin/max approach. Preferences for individual metrics and probability levels varied among radiation oncologists, centers and treatment sites. Conclusion: Probabilistic evaluation metrics are expected to be clinically usable and an improvement over current methods by the interviewed radiation oncologists. Further consensus and clinical validation are needed before widespread clinical implementation.

entries.title: Colloquium: Isotopes for medicine and fundamental physics
entries.abstract: Isotopes, variants of elements distinguished by their neutron number, have important applications for medicine and fundamental science. This review explores the historical challenges and new technologies for enriching and detecting isotopes. We motivate the work by challenges posed by three of history's greatest scientists: James Clerk Maxwell's thought experiment on thermodynamics, Ernest Rutherford's practical dilemma in radiochemistry, and Albert Einstein's questions about the probabilistic nature of quantum mechanics. The journey to meet these challenges has catalyzed the development of innovative techniques for isotope separation. These advancements can mitigate the worldwide crisis in the supply of enriched isotopes. We then explore the expected impact of these new technologies on medicine, which include radioisotopes for cancer therapy and stable isotopes as tracers for metabolism. We explain the importance of developing scalable techniques for isotope detection and how it can help with early detection of certain diseases. Finally, we turn to basic science, outlining proposed new tests of quantum mechanics that utilize radioactive atomic clocks to probe the fundamental nature of determinism and distinguishability of atoms.

entries.title: ShEPhERD-score: Fast, adaptable three-dimensional alignment of molecular features
entries.abstract: Three-dimensional (3D) molecular similarity scoring and alignment are widely employed in ligand-based virtual screening and molecular design, and are increasingly used for training and evaluating machine learning models. Existing open-source methods utilize various molecular representations spanning shape, electrostatics, pharmacophores, and hybrid representations, but their implementations as independent software packages with distinct application programming interfaces (APIs), optimizers, and limited GPU support make them difficult to compare, combine, or extend. Here, we develop ShEPhERD-score into a unified, modular platform for differentiable 3D molecular similarity scoring and alignment by combining diverse molecular representations with high-performance Numba CPU and Triton GPU kernels to support both large-scale library screening and pairwise similarity workflows. In matched comparisons with open-source 3D similarity tools on the DUDE-Z virtual screening benchmark, ShEPhERD-score performed comparably or better in eight of nine cases. Across the scoring modes in ShEPhERD-score, throughput ranges from 17,800 to 1.03 million alignments/second for ten-million-conformer libraries using a single NVIDIA L40S GPU. Moreover, we found that the most effective scoring mode varied by protein target, indicating that target-specific calibration against validation data may be valuable before large-scale screening and underscoring the need for a unified platform that provides diverse molecular representations. Together, these capabilities establish ShEPhERD-score as a single, extensible toolkit for rapid virtual screening and machine learning workflows.

entries.title: Prognosis Without Prediction: The Intrinsic Geometry of Survival
entries.abstract: Modeling systemic failure in high-dimensional environments is fundamentally limited by supervised algorithms that attempt to predict sparse, noisy or censored endpoints. To break this reliance on explicit outcome regression, we engineered the Self-Organizing Survival Manifolds (SOSM) framework, a deep learning architecture that decouples unsupervised representation learning from survival labels and treats time-to-event progression as an emergent geometric property. The system projects heterogeneous multi-omics arrays into a unified latent space governed by a pseudotime-weighted, curvature-minimizing graph Laplacian, organizing patient trajectories along low-dissipation geodesic flows. To validate the framework, we applied this architecture to a 184-patient clear cell renal cell carcinoma multi-omics cohort. Across a deterministic 5-fold cross-validation pipeline, SOSM achieved a mean Concordance Index of $0.768 \pm 0.068$, while out-of-fold risk stratification yielded significant survival divergence (log-rank $p < 0.001$) accompanied by a 14.7% increase in local manifold dissipation among high-risk patients. Furthermore, interrogating the network's encoder weights confirmed that the model autonomously recovered canonical metabolic and microenvironmental drivers of disease progression without supervised feature selection. By demonstrating that systemic failure can be mapped as a geometric phase transition, SOSM establishes a generalizable computational engine for prognostic modeling across biological, industrial and financial complex systems.

entries.title: Horizontal Flow Matching for Single-Cell Spatiotemporal Dynamics
entries.abstract: Learning the spatiotemporal dynamics of cells from spatial transcriptomics requires connecting snapshots of different cells acquired in different coordinate frames. A rotation or translation of a section can appear as cell movement and distort the inferred correspondence. We introduce horizontal flow matching, which learns changes in tissue organization, molecular state, and cell abundance up to shared rigid motion. The dynamics follow a continuity--reaction equation whose action assigns no cost to shared rigid motion, and the resulting horizontal projector removes this component from spatial prediction errors during learning and from predicted velocities during generation. An equivalent endpoint problem jointly estimates correspondence and relative pose in Wasserstein--Fisher--Rao geometry and yields analytic paths whose velocity and growth serve as regression targets. Regressing these targets recovers the horizontal dynamics under ideal population conditions. Our model, HORIZON, uses an equivariant transformer to predict velocity and growth from the current tissue, so that a tissue can be generated continuously from a single initial snapshot. On a simulated tissue observed in perturbed coordinate frames, alignment improves reconstruction and projection reduces rigid drift. On four spatial transcriptomics time courses, HORIZON reconstructs tissue geometry, gene expression, and cell abundance more accurately than existing spatial and unbalanced trajectory methods, and interpolates held-out developmental stages.

entries.title: Elysium: Simulation-Free Unbalanced Schrödinger Bridges
entries.abstract: Reconstructing cellular dynamics from snapshots is challenging because the destructive nature of single-cell measurements makes tracking the same cells over time impossible. Cellular dynamics are inherently stochastic and involve changes in population size through proliferation and apoptosis. Growth-based methods represent population change as a rate on the density, which does not assign exits and entries to individual cells. Unbalanced Schrödinger bridges model individual events, but neural solvers for killed diffusion bridges simulate trajectories during training. We introduce Elysium, a simulation-free solver that jointly learns state transition and mass change. Using a killed Brownian reference and its time reversal, Elysium constructs direct regression objectives from an optimal endpoint coupling and conditional bridge distributions, without simulating trajectories during training. We show that the minimizers of the expected training objectives recover the optimal unbalanced Schrödinger bridge. Empirically, Elysium reconstructs state transitions, population size, and event distributions on simulated benchmarks with known killed-diffusion ground truth, outperforming existing deterministic and bridge-based solvers. On single-cell time courses, it interpolates cell state distributions at unobserved time points, tracks population expansion and contraction, and captures biphasic drug-response dynamics.

entries.title: Chemotactic aggregation as cue-mediated adaptation toward Nash equilibrium in a spatial patterning game
entries.abstract: Chemotactic cells generate their own chemical gradients to form spatial patterns that support collective functions ranging from cooperative metabolism to immunity. Despite progress in understanding the optimality of chemotaxis in imposed chemical gradients, it remains unclear how close decentralized cell populations can come to maximizing the population-wide benefit of spatial organization through individual movement and local modulation of chemical gradients. We employ mean field game theory to characterize efficient spatial patterns achievable by decentralized populations as Nash equilibria: each agent optimizes its positioning given the spatial density of the other cells, whereas the population density is determined by the positioning of all individuals. We derive coupled dynamics of population movement and cue modulation that drive adaptation toward these equilibria and verify its structural correspondence to established phenomenological models of chemotactic pattern formation. We apply our framework to self-organized aggregation and numerically demonstrate that the dynamics can form multiple equilibrium patterns, some of which are comparable to the population-level optimum under moderate incentives to aggregate. We also show that the relative timescales of cue modulation and movement influence pattern selection and population-level efficiency: slower cue modulation can yield more coherent and efficient equilibrium patterns. Our framework thus highlights fundamental limits on collective optimization in decentralized cell populations, and suggests a functional role for timescales in self-organized coordination through environmental feedback.

entries.title: Biases and Limits of AlphaFold Predictions for Non-Globular Proteins
entries.abstract: AlphaFold has transformed protein structure prediction, making structural models accessible across the life sciences. We explore experimentally validated cases of non-globular proteins to uncover where predictions diverge from biologically relevant structural states and how molecular context shapes these discrepancies, guiding a more informed interpretation of AlphaFold models.

entries.title: Unmyelinated axons alter the biological interpretation of MRI biomarkers of demyelination
entries.abstract: Quantitative MRI methods are widely used to probe white matter microstructure; yet diffusion- and relaxation-based metrics are often interpreted primarily in terms of myelinated axons, implicitly assuming a negligible contribution from unmyelinated axons. Here, combining diffusion MRI (dMRI), relaxation-based MRI, and electron microscopy (EM) in the cuprizone mouse model of demyelination and recovery, we examine how unmyelinated axons shape MRI-derived microstructural indices, including axonal water fraction and $g$-ratio. To enable quantitative cellular-level comparisons, we developed automated tools for instance-level EM segmentation of white matter, allowing morphological analysis of myelinated and unmyelinated axonal populations. We find that, in the mouse model, diffusion-derived estimates of axonal water fraction reflect contributions from both axonal populations at sufficiently short diffusion times; accounting for unmyelinated axons removes an apparent bias and reveals that this metric corresponds to the total intra-axonal space rather than myelinated fibers alone. Similarly, MRI-derived $g$-ratio estimates correlate strongly with EM only when both axonal populations are included. We further demonstrate that within-voxel $g$-ratio heterogeneity introduces a systematic negative bias of up to $8\%$, increasing with the fraction of unmyelinated axons and variability in myelin thickness. Together, these findings change the biological interpretation of MRI biomarkers during demyelination by demonstrating that unmyelinated axons are a major determinant of MRI-derived white matter indices and that combining diffusion and relaxation contrasts enables a more accurate and interpretable quantification of demyelination. They further highlight the need for quantitative biomarkers that account for axonal heterogeneity in both health and disease.

entries.title: From real to synthetic: PSG-GAN learns sleep apnea signal dynamics for AI training
entries.abstract: Synthetic polysomnography (PSG) data has great potential in healthcare applications, for example in substituting real data that is sensitive and challenging to collect. Previous research on synthetic PSG data has been largely focused on short segments of individual signals, overlooking the inter-signal dynamics related to sleep disorders. In this study, we developed a generative adversarial network (PSG-GAN) for co-synthesizing longer segments of multiple PSG signals with diverse and complex characteristics typical of obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). The synthetic signals appeared realistic, and the electroencephalography and electrooculography band powers were similarly distributed across sleep stages. Moreover, the PSG-GAN learned to mirror signal interactions such as changes in photoplethysmography-based heart rate during and after breathing obstructions. An automatic scoring model trained solely with automatically scored synthetic signals reached good performance on sleep staging (\k{appa}=0.71 and 0.63) and respiratory event segmentation (\k{appa}=0.57 and 0.60), on two test sets consisting of healthy volunteers and OSA patients, respectively. This demonstrates the potential of synthetic data in supporting algorithm development for sleep diagnostics. The source code is available at https://github.com/rikuhuttunen/psg-gan.

entries.title: Impact-Based Analysis Method (IBAM) to evaluate the primary stability of the pedicle screw: A proof of concept
entries.abstract: The long-term success of spinal instrumentation depends on the initial stability of pedicle screws (PS), yet current intraoperative assessments rely on surgeon subjectivity. This study introduces a quantitative, non-invasive approach-the Impact-Based Analysis Method (IBAM)-to support intraoperative decision-making. The IBAM measures screw stability using low-amplitude impacts delivered with an instrumented hammer on the surgical screwdriver after screw insertion. An IBAM indicator, defined as the average time difference between the two earliest local maxima in the force signal, was analyzed under varying stability conditions in artificial bone samples. Experimental factors included bone density ($ρ$), insertion depth ( D ), and pilot hole diameter ( $Φ$ ). The IBAM indicator was compared with the PS pull-out force for each configuration. Although the main effects showed opposite trends for the pull-out force and the IBAM indicator, their relative magnitudes were similar ( $ρ$ $\sim$35%, D $\sim$25%, $Φ$ $\sim$15%). The relationship between the pull-out force and the IBAM indicator followed a power-law model (adjusted R 2 =___0.85) with a negative exponent. As screw stability increased, the pull-out force rose while the IBAM indicator decreased, demonstrating complementary sensitivity to bone-implant interface changes. While results are promising, the simplified experimental design limited the ability to fully capture bone-implant interaction complexity. Future studies should aim to validate IBAM in vivo to confirm its clinical applicability..

entries.title: Micrograph B-factor estimation via Wilson statistics
entries.abstract: The single-particle cryo-electron microscopy imaging process is known to cause exponential decay in the amplitude and power spectra of proteins. This decay is modeled by the B factor and is currently corrected as a post-processing stage of the 3D reconstruction. As a consequence, all experimental images in the dataset are assumed to share the same B factor. In this paper, we suggest a novel approach wherein the B factor is determined and corrected as a preprocessing step to the reconstruction. We show such an approach can improve reconstruction resolution.

entries.title: SCOPE: Single-Cell Omics Prediction from Histology via RNA-Protein Prior Enhancement
entries.abstract: Predicting the RNA and protein content of cells from routine H&E images could extend spatial molecular profiling to existing slide archives. However, both H&E-spatial proteomics and H&E-spatial transcriptomics paired datasets are limited by the number of available markers and the insufficient availability of high-quality, cell-resolved data. We present SCOPE (Single-Cell Omics Prediction via RNA-protein prior Enhancement), a unified framework that leverages biologically complementary information between RNA and proteins to address the limited availability of single-omics supervision. Our key insight is that, although RNA and proteins represent distinct molecular modalities, their biological relationships provide valuable shared knowledge that can benefit single-omics prediction tasks. To this end, SCOPE introduces biologically informed biomarker priors to enhance shared gene-level representations, enabling knowledge transfer across RNA and protein modalities through gene-protein correspondence and molecular associations. By exploiting these complementary relationships, SCOPE enables both prediction tasks to benefit from a shared backbone enriched with cross-omics biological knowledge. Furthermore, its biomarker correlation design facilitates the prediction of unseen markers, extending spatially resolved molecular profiling beyond directly supervised targets. Across test datasets spanning 16 organs, SCOPE improves the average RNA Pearson correlation over the strongest baseline by 8.8%. On two external protein cohorts, it improves the average Pearson correlation over the strongest baseline by 9.7% for seen markers and 11.9% for unseen markers.

entries.title: MitoWorld: A Stochastic World Model of the Single-Cell Cycle under Genetic Perturbation
entries.abstract: A cell observed after a gene knockdown has an uncertain future, both in how its appearance will evolve and when it will divide. Existing approaches predict endpoints or population-level changes without jointly modeling individual trajectories and division timing. In this work, we present MitoWorld, a stochastic world model that generates these future appearances as continuous evolution in a Gaussian reference latent, terminated by a division hazard and converted into images by a conditional diffusion renderer. The ordinary transition provably preserves its Gaussian reference, tying its noise to its dynamics; paired observations identify its discrete transition where stationary marginals cannot. The hazard turns division timing into a survival likelihood that can be tested against real cycle lengths. On 325 held-out MitoCheck tracks spanning 17 knockdowns and a control, MitoWorld lowers FID by 34.6\% and the video metric JEDi by 45.6\% relative to the strongest baselines. Its latent-space prediction intervals achieve near-nominal 90\% coverage, are 35\% narrower than those of a model with freely fitted noise. The hazard also yields cell-cycle length distributions with KS distance close to the model-based finite-sample reference. Testable single-cell stochastic dynamics thus offer a generative tool for time-lapse perturbation screens.

entries.title: Cardiac MRI-informed electrocardiography enables biologically grounded cardiomyopathy detection
entries.abstract: Precise myocardial phenotyping at population scale is limited by the cost and accessibility of cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR), whereas electrocardiography (ECG) is widely available but reflects electrical rather than structural and functional information. Here we develop MyoECG, a cross-modal representation learning framework that distils myocardial structural and functional knowledge from CMR into standard 12-lead ECGs, enabling imaging-informed cardiomyopathy detection and subtype classification from ECGs alone. MyoECG was pretrained on 45,241 paired ECG-CMR examinations from UK Biobank and a tertiary cardiovascular centre, then developed and validated across more than 1.8 million ECGs from seven independent datasets. Across internal and external datasets spanning prevalences of 0.2-54.7%, MyoECG outperformed five pretrained ECG foundation models, with AUROCs of 0.800-0.974 for cardiomyopathy detection. In a multi-reader study of six cardiologists, MyoECG assistance improved mean sensitivity by 0.109 (95% CI, 0.041-0.175; P = 0.009) and specificity by 0.056 (95% CI, 0.004-0.108; P = 0.040). In 41,128 UK Biobank participants, the MyoECG score showed genetic correlations with cardiomyopathy (rg = 0.409) and dilated cardiomyopathy (rg = 0.371), genome-wide associations at four loci, including regions mapped to NFIA and KCNQ1, and associations with 69 circulating proteins related to myocardial stress, cell adhesion, vascular biology and metabolism. The cardiomyopathy correlation attenuated to non-significance after adjustment for 27 measured CMR traits (rg = 0.131; P = 0.143), indicating that the score captures CMR-derived information rather than dataset-specific shortcuts. MyoECG offers a scalable route to CMR-informed cardiomyopathy assessment and a strategy for transferring knowledge from resource-intensive imaging to widely deployable physiological signals.

entries.title: A structure-based model of the bacterial chemosensory array reveals how the scaffolding protein CheW tunes sensory responses
entries.abstract: We introduce a structure-based Ising model of the bacterial chemosensory array to investigate how the scaffolding protein CheW tunes signaling responses. The model couples the activity states of core signaling units and of CheW subunits within hexameric rings on a lattice with the structure observed in cryoEM experiments. Recent experiments show that increasing CheW participation in hexameric rings raises response cooperativity in non-adapting cells and sensitivity in adaptation-proficient cells. Our lattice model quantitatively reproduces both effects, while mean-field theory shows that CheW increases the effective coupling between core units, sharpening the response in both cell types. The statistics of CheW placement (complete hexameric rings versus random distribution) substantially alter how responses vary with CheW abundance. Moreover, different coupling strengths can yield the same static response yet markedly different activity fluctuations and dynamics. CheW abundance further controls a crossover from relaxational to oscillatory fluctuations, whose location depends on the spatial distribution of CheW. These dynamical signatures, including oscillations predicted near native CheW levels, are testable by single-cell dynamics measurements. Combined with CheW titration and our modeling results, these measurements can probe the array's assembly dynamics and allosteric couplings. Beyond the chemosensory array, our approach can generalize to other large protein complexes, providing a framework to study the functional role of scaffolding proteins and allosteric interfaces in signal processing.

entries.title: Benchmarking Traditional and Learning-Based Reference-Free Compressors for Long-Read Sequencing Data
entries.abstract: Long-read sequencing technologies generate large volumes of data, creating substantial storage and transmission demands. Although reference-based compressors can achieve high compression, their reliance on an appropriate reference genome limits their use. We present LRCBench, a benchmark and survey of reference-free lossless compressors for long-read sequencing data. We review traditional and learning-based general-purpose and sequencing-specific methods, then evaluate 35 compressors on 16 real-world datasets from Oxford Nanopore and PacBio platforms. We compare compression ratio, storage savings, runtime, peak memory use, and robustness across datasets. Learning-based compressors are evaluated on six MinION datasets because of their high computational costs. CoLoRd achieves the best overall compression ratios in our experiments, while other methods offer trade-offs in speed, memory use, and robustness. We also examine multithreaded speedup and discuss future directions in parallel acceleration, privacy protection, adaptive parameter tuning, and hardware-algorithm co-design.

entries.title: Geometry-bridge flow matching for blind rigid-motion correction in head cone-beam CT
entries.abstract: Rigid motion of a patient head during head cone-beam CT (CBCT) scan can degrade image quality and complicate recovery of accurate anatomical structures from the measured projections. We present a 3D flow-matching prior approach that learns the image changes induced by motion. Its geometry-bridge connects motion-corrupted and motion-free Feldkamp-Davis-Kress (FDK) reconstructed images of the same source volume through progressively reduced simulated motion. The forward projector's geometry derivative supplies analytic velocity targets along this path. A plug-and-play loop encompasses the learned image updates together with spline-based pose estimation, conjugate-gradient data consistency, and image total-variation regularization. Both the refined image volume and the FDK reconstructed image volume at the estimated poses are evaluated. On simulated 360-view scans from 30 held-out CQ500 patients with nominal per-component motion amplitudes within 10 mm / 10 degrees, the framework achieved state-of-the-art image reconstruction quality and motion accuracy in comparison with other methos such as learned autofocus and diffusion-based joint reconstruction. Mean peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) reached 37.1 dB and mean detector-plane reprojection error (RPE) was 0.27 mm. With matched endpoints at the inference settings, the geometry bridge improved PSNR by 1.6 dB and reduced RPE by 33% relative to image-linear training. With 50 prior updates and coarse-to-fine motion estimation, total processing time averaged 9.1 minutes per patient on an RTX A6000.

entries.title: STORM: A Lightweight Structure-Free Model for Binding Affinity Prediction
entries.abstract: Accurately predicting a small molecule's binding affinity to a protein, a critical task in drug discovery, remains challenging. Physics-based approaches like free-energy perturbation (FEP) have very high computational costs and require expert setup. Recent machine learning--based cofolding models have reported accuracy approaching that of FEP---and at least one of them, Boltz-2, has already been widely adopted for affinity prediction---but they remain expensive for large computational screens and even more expensive for retraining on newly collected experimental data. To address these challenges, we introduce STORM: Similarity Transfer from Observed Reference Molecules. STORM is a fast, simple machine learning model that ensembles many small model fusions of diverse protein and molecule representations for binding affinity prediction. Trained on the same data, STORM matches or exceeds the accuracy of Boltz-2 on multiple evaluation datasets, while delivering a speed improvement of over five orders of magnitude for both inference and training. Our results also suggest opportunities to substantially improve affinity prediction accuracy by integrating historical experimental affinity data with structural and biophysical information.

entries.title: Deep-Learning-Assisted Full Waveform Inversion for Attenuation Reconstruction in Ultrasound Computed Tomography
entries.abstract: Acoustic attenuation is more challenging to reconstruct and has received less attention than sound speed in ultrasound computed tomography using full-waveform inversion (FWI). In this study, a deep-learning (DL)-assisted FWI framework was proposed for attenuation reconstruction based on our previous work. Some numerical experiments were conducted to investigate the strategy and the effectiveness of using DL to help accelerate and improve the reconstruction quality of attenuation imaging in FWI. The results indicated that DL saved computational cost by 28% and improved attenuation reconstruction accuracy by 70% when combined with sufficiently accurate sound speed estimates. The result supports the potential of DL initialization to improve the computational efficiency and reconstruction quality of joint SOS and attenuation FWI.

entries.title: Quantitative Modeling of Action-Potential-Driven Sodium Dynamics in Neurons: From Sodium Influx to Sodium MRI
entries.abstract: Neuronal action potentials are accompanied by the influx of extracellular sodium ions (Na+) into axons through voltage-gated sodium channels. Repetitive neuronal firing can lead to activity-dependent increases in intracellular sodium concentration, which are subsequently reversed primarily through the Na+/K+-ATPase. Quantifying these dynamic changes provides a biophysical foundation for investigating neuronal activity using sodium (23Na) magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). This mini-review examines the relationships among firing frequency, action-potential-driven sodium influx, and intracellular sodium accumulation, to establish a quantitative framework linking neuronal activity to sodium MRI. The potential sensitivity and limitation of conventional and compartment-sensitive sodium MRI for detecting activity-dependent sodium changes are also discussed. Keywords: Sodium MRI; neuronal firing; action potential; sodium influx; intracellular sodium concentration.

entries.title: Structured AI ideation yields physical strategies for epithelial barrier repair
entries.abstract: AI systems increasingly support literature analysis, candidate evaluation and hypothesis refinement, but enabling researchers to explore research directions beyond established disciplinary approaches remains challenging. We developed Abelio, an AI system designed to generate novel research directions by expanding investigators' avenues of inquiry. Abelio reformulates research objectives, uses these alternative formulations to identify relevant elements outside conventional disciplinary boundaries, and refines the resulting hypotheses. Each stage integrates divergent exploration with convergent selection through a dedicated subsystem. In quantitative evaluations, proposals generated by the Ideation Core (Abelio's hypothesis-generation core) outperformed those of four frontier large language models in scientific soundness and hypothesis diversity, and three of four in distance from existing literature. Subsystem ablation showed that each subsystem contributes to the property it targets, with the contribution of Element Selection measurable before Refinement. To investigate intestinal epithelial barrier restoration, Abelio proposed physical interventions involving membrane-tethered poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) and cholesterol-anchored complementary DNA. Both proposals were archived before experimentation and subsequently tested independently in damaged Caco-2 monolayers. PEG preserved barrier function in a membrane-surface-dependent manner, whereas complementary DNA enabled sequence-specific restoration that was reversible on demand. These findings demonstrate how structured research ideation can identify experimentally testable approaches beyond established disciplinary conventions.

entries.title: Fiberpose: state-of-the-art fiber morphometry and instance segmentation with a distance-transform neural network
entries.abstract: Analysis of fibrous structures in SEM images is a routine task in biomedical engineering and materials science. However, most available methods for fiber quantification still rely on classical image binarization followed by simple post-processing. These approaches often produce unreliable results in images with weak boundaries, heterogeneous contrast, and densely packed fibers. Here, we introduce Fiberpose, a framework that reformulates fiber analysis as direct regression of a smooth distance-transform (DT) field, together with a novel set of geometry-based algorithms specifically adapted to this representation. The predicted field directly encodes fiber geometry, while the accompanying algorithms enable instance reconstruction and measurement of diameter and orientation within a unified workflow. The framework is implemented as a standalone Python desktop application and a web tool https://fiberpose.org. On an independent dataset of fibrous SEM images, Fiberpose achieved state-of-the-art instance-segmentation accuracy in comparison with SAM2 and Cellpose-SAM, and more accurate diameter measurements than DiameterJ, Fibar and GIFT. The method remains effective in dense and weakly contrasted regions and shows qualitative generalization across microscopy modalities not represented in the training data. Fiberpose therefore provides an interpretable geometric representation and an automated pipeline for reproducible quantitative characterization of fibrous materials.

entries.title: Optimising Recruitment and Sample Allocation in Multi-Site Rare Disease Studies
entries.abstract: Clinical research in rare diseases is challenged by the limited availability and broad geographical distribution of eligible patients. This necessitates multi-centre collaboration and strategic selection of analytical laboratories based on capacity, cost, and capability. We present a mathematical framework based on cardinality optimisation to support key operational decisions in study design, balancing clinical relevance, feasibility, budgetary constraints, and logistical factors. The framework was implemented in the Reconstruction and Computational Modelling for Inherited Metabolic Diseases (Recon4IMD) project, aiming to recruit 1,900 diagnosed patients across 24 healthcare centres and eight metabolomic laboratories. Compared to both proportional heuristic and greedy marginal allocation baselines, the proposed optimisation model consistently achieved higher recruitment yields in simulated multi-centre scenarios and reduced metabolomic analysis costs by approximately 30% under unconstrained conditions. Notably, both the heuristic and greedy allocation baselines became infeasible under progressively tighter laboratory capacity constraints, whereas the optimised model maintained feasibility and cost control. These findings highlight the value of integrated optimisation strategies for improving recruitment, platform selection, and sample allocation in complex, resource-limited research settings.

entries.title: Feedback and Resource Competition in Incoherent Feedforward Loops: When Is Cumulative Dose Ordering Preserved?
entries.abstract: Biochemical coupling can change the expression levels and timing predicted by an incoherent feedforward loop (IFFL) model without changing cumulative dose ordering. We derive ordering conditions using shared-production identities and Metzler comparison bounds, with tail guarantees beyond finite computation. A nonlinear example exhibits delayed slope reversal at a fixed dose, on an $O(1/η)$ timescale as pathway mismatch $η$ vanishes. At one fixed joint fit, validated bounds establish decreasing cumulative output across 20-100 ng nominal burden, from zero to full target loading, at every positive finite observation time for a translation-blocking model and an RNA-decay model. Full loading at 20 ng reduces 48-hour cumulative output by 13.35% and 10.18%, respectively, while endpoint concentration in the first model changes by only +0.15%. Preserved ordering therefore does not ensure quantitative agreement.

entries.title: Molecular memory reduces timing noise in stochastic gene expression
entries.abstract: Fluctuations in gene expression affect the timing precision of downstream events triggered when a gene product reaches a critical threshold. The first-passage time (FPT) to this threshold characterizes the timing of such events. In conventional single-step birth--death models, reaction waiting times are exponentially distributed and hence memoryless. In this setting, FPT noise exhibits a U-shaped dependence on the threshold, attaining its minimum near one-half of the steady-state mean. However, mRNA production and degradation often involve multiple sequential steps, leading to hypoexponential distributions of mRNA production times and mRNA lifetimes. Here, we investigate how molecular memory arising from multistep mRNA production and degradation affects FPT statistics in bursty gene expression. We calculate FPT statistics in the small-noise limit. Both multistep mechanisms reduce FPT noise, but through distinct mechanisms. Multistep burst arrival reduces mRNA copy-number fluctuations, thereby suppressing timing noise. Multistep degradation instead reshapes transient accumulation dynamics, reducing relative timing noise even when steady-state mRNA noise increases. The threshold that minimizes FPT noise remains close to one-half of the steady-state mean, except for multistep burst arrival with constant burst sizes, for which it shifts to lower values. Stochastic simulations support the analytical predictions within their regimes of validity and show that these qualitative conclusions persist beyond the small-noise approximation.

entries.title: ST-FateFlow: Continuous Gene-Spatial Reconstruction with Differentiation-Potential Learning from Time-Resolved Spatial Transcriptomics
entries.abstract: Time-resolved spatial transcriptomics provides a powerful view of dynamic biological processes by measuring cellular states together with their spatial organization across time. However, destructive profiling and experimental cost restrict observations to a few discrete time points collected from independent samples, with no known cell pairing across time. This makes it difficult to reconstruct gene expression and tissue organization at unobserved stages and to characterize differentiation-associated dynamics. Here, we introduce ST-FateFlow, a flow-matching framework for continuous gene-spatial dynamics and differentiation-potential learning. ST-FateFlow jointly learns gene-expression and spatial-coordinate velocity fields, enabling interpolation of missing time points and continuous modeling of transcriptional evolution and tissue remodeling. In parallel, it independently learns a time-conditioned differentiation potential, whose values organize cell states along inferred differentiation progressions and support the analysis of differentiation-associated transcriptional changes. Across multiple time-resolved spatial transcriptomics datasets, ST-FateFlow effectively captures coordinated gene-expression and spatial dynamics. Case studies further show that the learned potential landscapes are consistent with known developmental and regenerative trajectories and help identify candidate genes associated with differentiation progression.

entries.title: Discovery of new antiviral agents through artificial intelligence: in vitro and in vivo results
entries.abstract: In this research, we employed a deep reinforcement learning (RL)-based molecule design platform to generate a diverse set of compounds targeting the neuraminidase (NA) of influenza A and B viruses. A total of 60291 compounds were generated, of which 86.5% displayed superior physicochemical properties compared to oseltamivir. After narrowing down the selection through computational filters, nine compounds with non-sialic acid-like structures were selected for in vitro experiments. We identified two compounds, DS-22-inf-009 and DS-22-inf-021 that effectively inhibited the NAs of both influenza A and B viruses (IAV and IBV), including H275Y mutant strains at low micromolar concentrations. Molecular dynamics simulations revealed a similar pattern of interaction with amino acid residues as oseltamivir. In cell-based assays, DS-22-inf-009 and DS-22-inf-021 inhibited IAV and IBV in a dose-dependent manner with EC50 values ranging from 0.29 uM to 2.31 uM. Furthermore, animal experiments showed that both DS-22-inf-009 and DS-22-inf-021 exerted antiviral activity in mice, conferring 65% and 85% protection from IAV (H1N1 pdm09), and 65% and 100% protection from IBV (Yamagata lineage), respectively. Thus, these findings demonstrate the potential of RL to generate compounds with promising antiviral properties.
entries.comment: Accepted manuscript. 13 pages, 5 figures; supplementary material included (supplementary text, Tables S1-S2, Figures S1-S5). Published in Antiviral Research 222 (2024) 105818

entries.title: OCCAM: Improved Single-Cell Representation Learning and Perturbation Effect Prediction
entries.abstract: Predicting the effects of genetic perturbations requires models that generalize beyond observed cell contexts and gene combinations. We introduce Occam, a multilayer perceptron (MLP) framework for representation learning and perturbation-effect prediction. Occam combines cell representations learned through denoising with gene interaction, text, and protein-sequence features. It achieves the highest aggregate representation scores for perturbation information and cell-type preservation with batch integration. In cross-context few-shot prediction, a perturbation and a cell context are each observed during training, but never together. Occam better captures the measured response patterns for these unobserved combinations than four retrained competitors or direct transfer of the same perturbation's measured effects from other training cell lines. Without fine-tuning, Occam best distinguishes perturbations among the evaluated models and simple baselines in cell lines held out from predictor training, across seen and unseen assays. Predicting expression levels accurately in these settings remains challenging. For double perturbations, which target two genes simultaneously, Occam composes learned single-gene responses to better capture the combined response and reduce expression error compared with competing models and summed single-gene effects. These gains extend to both strongly additive and weakly additive responses. Together, these results support simple MLPs for cell representation learning and perturbation-effect prediction across contexts and gene combinations.

entries.title: Diversity Preservation Recovers Transcription Factor Motifs Across Challenging Confounder Landscapes
entries.abstract: Motif discovery is a process where DNA sequences are searched for the short patterns, called motifs, that transcription factor (TF) proteins bind. However, the motif lengths are often unknown and motif attribution often competes with a near-identical motif of a related protein. In this work, we pair a motif genotype whose length emerges from an evolvable gate with MAP-Elites archives organized by three descriptor pairs, and validate every motif against the full HOCOMOCO database. On five liver ChIP-seq datasets spanning distinct confounder landscapes, a $(μ + λ)$ baseline differing only in survivor selection collapses onto a single motif and never ranks the target first across three datasets, while every MAP-Elites archive does so in at least 13 of 30 seeds on every dataset. Against the motif discovery tool MEME, run on the same sequences and validated identically, the archives recover the target signal as reliably on four datasets and more robustly when motif width is constrained. Neither method ranks the target above its closest relatives on HNF4A and JUND over the full width range, but narrow archive motifs rank HNF4A first in up to 43% of seeds, where MEME misses the motif in all settings. Diversity preservation improves our ability to recover consistent motif signal, although motif annotation remains a challenging problem for all methods we tested.

entries.title: Rule-based curation and validation in batch fermentation of a genome-scale metabolic model of the mycoprotein fungus Fusarium venenatum A3/5
entries.abstract: Sustainable protein supply is a central food-system challenge, and mycoprotein from Fusarium venenatum is an established, low-impact option. Its production relies on refined glucose, and yields on lower-cost feedstocks are normally found by fermentation. Genome-scale metabolic models (GEMs) can estimate these yields before any experiment, but to our knowledge none has been published for this fungus, and models transferred from related species inherit template errors. Here we built iJL1143, a GEM of strain A3/5, from an Aspergillus niger model and curated it with rules based on homology, thermodynamics and the literature. We compared it with the uncurated Draft model in four oxygen-enriched batch fermentations on glucose and fructose. Thermodynamic directionality rules and the direction of the mitochondrial GTP/GDP carrier brought the maximum ATP yield of the Draft model within the theoretical range. As a result, with sequential sugar uptake and no fitted parameters, the mean final-biomass discrepancy fell from 20% for the Draft model to 6% for iJL1143. Sequential uptake and a fitted lag time also reduced its biomass time-course error from 4.88 to 0.42 g/L. In oxygen-enriched batch fermentation, iJL1143 can therefore estimate obtainable biomass before fermentation, which could reduce the experiments needed to develop lower-cost mycoprotein.
entries.comment: 20 pages, 5 figures, 2 tables; Supplementary material included

entries.title: Pharmaco-mechanical computational simulation of atherosclerotic arteries: effects of calcium channel blockers on local stress distributions
entries.abstract: This paper presents a computational model integrating transmural drug transport, smooth muscle cell contraction, nonlinear anisotropic material behavior, and residual stresses to investigate the effects of calcium channel blockers~(CCBs) on local stress distributions in atherosclerotic arteries. The balance of linear momentum is coupled with a three-dimensional reaction-diffusion equation for the drug transport. Smooth muscle contraction is modeled phenomenologically based on a chemo-mechanical model that incorporates the effects of stretch on intracellular calcium dynamics and calcium sensitization. A novel drug-tissue interaction model is proposed to capture the effects of CCBs on intracellular calcium and thus on smooth muscle contraction. Material parameters are identified by fitting to experimental data from the literature and finite element simulations are conducted on five exemplary atherosclerotic arterial geometries reconstructed from histological cross-sections. Simulation results show that although CCBs reduce the stresses in the media through reduced smooth muscle contraction, they shift load to the fibrous cap, whose stress increases in all five geometries (median of up to 28.9~kPa). This increase varies strongly between plaque morphologies and becomes smaller with lower smooth muscle tone before treatment, lower drug concentrations in the arterial wall and increasing axial pre-stretch. A blood pressure reduction of 10~mmHg already lowers it to a median of at most 3.8~kPa in four of the five geometries. Our findings suggest that CCBs may increase the rupture risk of vulnerable plaques with highly loaded fibrous caps under insufficient blood pressure reduction, which remains to be confirmed experimentally and clinically.

entries.title: Fluid exchange and renewal in the left atrial appendage
entries.abstract: Fluid exchange through the opening of a cavity does not uniquely determine how the cavity is washed out. We investigate this phenomenon in the left atrial appendage (LAA), a deforming side cavity of the heart, using simulations of 17 patient-specific atria with wall motion reconstructed from time-resolved computed tomography. Fluid exchange through the LAA ostium is decomposed into a component driven by LAA volume change and a component due to simultaneous bidirectional flow, with no net volume transport. Washout of a scalar initially confined to the LAA is compared with predictions from two well-mixed washout models and assessed alongside residence-time distributions. Volume-driven transport accounts for approximately 24-78% of total exchange across the simulated atria. Relative washout efficiencies are approximately 26-53% with respect to the inflow-driven washout model that assumes scalar-free inflow. A scalar-balance decomposition identifies two contributions to this discrepancy: re-ingestion of previously expelled scalar and preferential export of scalar-poor fluid. Both effects reduce the effective washout rate in every configuration. Residence-time distributions reveal coexisting distinct younger and older fluid regions, and a regional analysis of one appendage localizes the older population predominantly in its distal region. These findings show that substantial exchange across the LAA ostium coexists with prolonged distal retention. Effective renewal depends on how much fluid crosses the ostium and which fluid is exchanged.

entries.title: The relationship between junctional zone, smooth muscle tone and intra-uterine pressure
entries.abstract: The junctional zone is a thin low contrast region of the inner myometrium, visible on T2weighted MRI images. Investigators have long sought histologic particularities of this region. Here, we summarize evidence that this region's specific appearance is not due to a particular tissue composition, but is a reflection of underlying smooth muscle activity. Smooth muscle tone in the spirally fibered myometrium wrings out blood and interstitial fluids to create a static low-contrast T2 region around the myometrium, while phasic smooth muscle contractions create transient, propagative low-contrast waves. We show that the competition between centripetal inhibitory adrenergic innervation from the serosa and centrifugal excitatory hormonal gradients from the endometrium divides the uterus in a tonic inner-and a quiescent outer-region. Bridging MRI and manometry studies, we discuss the relation between smooth muscle activity and intra-uterine pressure. Dysregulation of nerve and/or hormonal activity can result in a thicker tonic smooth muscle layer, entailing a thicker junctional zone and high intrauterine pressures characteristic of dyscontractility in severe dysmenorrhea, endometriosis and adenomyosis.

entries.title: Calpha: Toward Native Biomolecular Intelligence in a General-Purpose Language Model
entries.abstract: Biomolecular foundation models predict the structures of proteins and their complexes accurately, and large language models (LLMs) reason in natural language, but the two remain separate: the abilities of the former are not part of a general-purpose LLM, and the reasoning of the latter does not enter a structure prediction. Calpha aims at one general model that folds proteins and complexes, understands protein sequence and structure, and lets its language reasoning influence the structures it predicts. This report covers the first step, in which an LLM outputs single-chain protein structures. Qwen3.5-9B reads a sequence enriched with ESM2 residue features. It can respond in text or emit a token that invokes a pretrained SimpleFold structure head, which receives information about the protein only through Qwen's residue states. Under a fixed folding request, the head achieves mean TM-scores of 0.808 on the FoldBench-334 development set, 0.635 on CASP16 domains and 0.900 on a CAMEO-style PDB set. We compare these predictions with a baseline in which ESM2-3B encodes the sequence and a fine-tuned SimpleFold-3B head predicts the coordinates. The two systems also differ in trainable weights, training duration and crop length. For chains of 100--299 residues, all three paired confidence intervals include zero. At 300--600 residues, the mean differences are -0.044, -0.160 and -0.025, respectively. In a separate test, four English request types triggered folding on every evaluated example. Protein training reduced accuracy on a 350-item MMLU-Pro subset from 77.4% to 70.3%. An LLM can therefore output single-chain structures from its own states, with lower long-chain scores in the current comparisons and reduced accuracy on the evaluated MMLU-Pro subset. Complex prediction, structure understanding and the effect of language reasoning on the predicted coordinates remain future work.

entries.title: A Soft Sponge-Pillar Electrode Platform for Motion-Tolerant Ambulatory EEG and Sleep Monitoring
entries.abstract: Long-term wearable electrophysiological recording systems are essential for both clinical and real-world environments. While a wide range of wearable devices have been reported for electrocardiogram (ECG) and electromyogram (EMG) recording applications, most electroencephalography (EEG) measurements still require subjects to remain stationary while wearing rigid and uncomfortable equipment. Here, a soft and wearable sponge pillar EEG electrode is presented for long-term and motion-tolerant EEG recording. The electrode is composed of two layers of a carbon black (CB)-polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) composite, where a firmer solid base assists in bypassing hair, enabling stable access to the scalp, while a porous sponge tip ensures comfort, reliable contact, and low skin-electrode impedance. Fabricated via a sugar templating process without microfabrication steps, the microporous sponge structure offers low modulus and significantly enhances the contact area with the skin when loaded with conductive gel. This allows the electrode to achieve a lower contact impedance of $1.62 \times 10^{4}\,Ω$ at 10 Hz, outperforming conventional gelled electrodes while maintaining gel stability for over 18 hours. With the electrodes integrated into wearable form factors such as headbands, headphones, and baseball caps, EEG signal recording during motion have been demonstrated, achieving a signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of 16.46 dB. These features establish the sponge pillar electrode as a promising platform for next generation wearable EEG systems, enabling comfortable, stable, and prolonged brain signal acquisition on ambulatory subjects and in naturalistic environments.
entries.comment: 37 pages, 5 figures, Supporting Information with 10 supplementary figures. Chansoo Kim and Weilun Li contributed equally to this work

entries.title: Using an instrumented hammer to predict the lateral hinge fracture in high tibial osteotomy: A cadaveric study
entries.abstract: Open-wedge High-Tibial Osteotomy is the most commonly employed technique addressing varus knee osteoarthritis. During this procedure, the osteotome passes through cortical and trabecular bone. A common complication is lateral hinge fractures, which depends upon when the surgeon stops impacting the osteotome. The aim of the present study is to determine whether an instrumented hammer can be employed to detect (i) the bone type (cortical or trabecular) surrounding the osteotome tip and (ii) when bone is fractured by the osteotome. Seventeen lower-limb specimens were obtained from nine fresh human anatomical subjects. The osteotome was impacted using the instrumented hammer until rupture. Each impact signal was recorded and analyzed. An algorithm was developed to detect the transitions between cortical and trabecular bone and vice versa. Detection was based on the relative variation of $τ$ derived from the force signal as a function of time as the time difference between the second___and___first impact peaks. The values of $τ$ were significantly lower in cortical bone compared to trabecular bone. Considering the arrival of the osteotome tip in trabecular bone during a medial, a difference of less than 2 impacts between the surgeon and the algorithm was obtained for 71% of the cases. For the lateral osteotomy it was obtained in 81% of the cases. This cadaveric study demonstrated that the instrumented hammer could prevent impacts leading to hinge rupture, which suggests that future clinical trials are warranted.

entries.title: Detecting the pterygomaxillary disjunction using an instrumented hammer: A cadaveric study
entries.abstract: Background: In many maxillofacial surgeries, the surgeon must perform a pterygomaxillary disjunction in order to separate the jaw from the skull. The disjunction is performed using an osteotome which is impacted with a hammer until its tip crosses through the pterygoid plates. To determine whether the disjunction has occurred and avoid complications, surgeons still rely on their proprioception. Methods: The aim of this study is to validate a vibroacoustic set-up constituted by an instrumented hammer equipped with a force sensor, aiming at detecting if the disjunction has occurred. To do so, fourteen osteotomies were performed in anatomical subject jaws. For each impact, the force signal was recorded and analyzed. A classification algorithm (Support Vector Machine method coupled with a cost matrix) was developed based on indicators extracted from the signal to determine whether the disjunction had occurred. Impacts were classified into two classes, one before and the other after the osteotome had crossed the pterygoid plates. To avoid undetected disjunctions a cost matrix was added to the algorithm. The coefficients from the matrix were chosen using by minimizing the Negative Likelihood Ratio. Findings: The algorithm was able to distinguish impacts before and after the disjunction with an accuracy of 96 %. Moreover, the instrumented hammer was able to detect the disjunction with a maximum delay of two impacts. Interpretation: These results pave the way for the development of a per-operative decision support system for the pterygomaxillary disjunction.

entries.title: Multimodal assessment of the skin biomechanical properties during wound healing and hyaluronic acid response
entries.abstract: Various methods such as elastography or mechanical testing have been developed to quantify the mechanical properties of soft tissues, which are related to the tissue local pathophysiological conditions. This study is the first one to investigate the in vivo performances of the Impact-Based Analysis Method (IBAM) to characterize the biomechanical behavior of skin during physiological mechanisms. A murine model (12 Sprague-Dawley rats) was considered and various measurements of skin mechanical properties were conducted on different regions of interest over a 3-week period. The effects of wound healing after full-thickness excisional wound and an intradermal hyaluronic acid (HA) injection were monitored using IBAM, as well as two commercially available devices: Cutometer__ and MyotonPro__. The indicators $Δ$t (from IBAM), R0 and R5 (from Cutometer__) vary significantly as a function of wound healing time, which corresponds to a stiffening of healing tissue compared to healthy tissue. The indicator $Δ$t and S (from MyotonPro__) are significantly different when HA was injected compared to healthy tissue, which also corresponds to less stiff tissue. Additionally, both IBAM and Cutometer__ detect significant biomechanical variations in superficial soft tissue related to tissue growth in all measurement regions. This first in vivo use of IBAM shows that IBAM could assess significant variations related to wound healing or regeneration mechanisms following HA injection. This study paves the way for the development of a simple, low-cost and objective device. Future clinical studies or other animal models should be carried out to confirm these results.

entries.title: multiCAsp: Spatially Informed Canonical Association Analysis of Multi-Omic Data
entries.abstract: Simultaneous profiling of multiple molecular layers at spatially resolved locations creates opportunities to identify shared cross-modal biological variation in its tissue context. We present multiCAsp (multi-omic Canonical Association informed by spatial graph), a probabilistic latent-factor model for integrating $M \geq 2$ spatially resolved omic modalities. It incorporates spatial dependence through a graph-Laplacian prior on shared latent factors and uses an expectation-maximization algorithm to estimate factor scores and modality-specific feature loadings. Because the prior is defined on a neighborhood graph rather than on Euclidean distances, it accommodates irregular tissue geometries and extends naturally to multiple tissue sections. Simulations show that multiCAsp consistently achieves higher mean latent subspace and loading recovery than alternative methods across varying sample sizes, feature dimensions, and noise levels, with the largest gains under high noise. Compared with an existing Gaussian process-based spatial factor model, it is also less sensitive to how the spatial coordinates are represented, produces spatially smoother factors, and has lower computational cost. Applied to metabolomic-proteomic data from macaque cortex and gene-protein data from human renal carcinoma, multiCAsp recovers spatially coherent multi-omic factors with interpretable biological signatures. In the macaque data, transferred factors retain broad spatial patterns across animals and support cross-modal prediction of protein abundances from metabolomic measurements.

entries.title: Weight-Space Programming Changes How an LLM Uses Python for Computational Biology
entries.abstract: Weight-space programming allows a language model to edit another model's weights without gradient-based training. We used Claude Opus 5.5 to edit Qwen3.5-0.8B and investigated how the edits changed its use of Python on computational biology problems. We compared four initial edited checkpoints with the original model on 50 test problems across three test seeds, yielding 600 paired evaluations. Strictly correct answers increased from 44 to 77, and technically correct answers, which included correct final values rejected for formatting, increased from 64 to 100. Repeated Python calls decreased from 1,834 to 1,044. Among the 64 pairs in which only the edited response was technically correct, the original model had already computed the correct value in 36 but did not submit a technically correct final answer. The edited model corrected the computation in 13 of the 64 pairs. With six additional checkpoints on the same 50 problems, technically correct answers rose from 96 to 154 across 900 pairs. We explored three selected problems with ten test seeds for each of ten checkpoints. On the melting-temperature problem, correct Python outputs decreased from 60 to 22 while technically correct final answers increased from 0 to 18. Weight editing changed both the calculations Qwen ran and whether it submitted a correct answer.
entries.comment: 16 pages, 3 figures, 6 main tables, and 1 supplementary table

entries.title: Dynamic infrared thermography and computed tomography angiography fusion for DIEP flap perforator selection: a novel measurement system
entries.abstract: Accurate perforator selection is critical for successful deep inferior epigastric artery perforator (DIEP) flap breast reconstruction. While computed tomography angiography (CTA) provides high-resolution anatomical detail, it lacks functional perfusion assessment. Dynamic infrared thermography (DIRT), in contrast, captures superficial rewarming dynamics but lacks objective anatomical validation. This study presents a standardized multimodal measurement system enabling automated fusion of DIRT with CTA-derived perforator coordinates. The framework integrates controlled thermographic acquisition, real-time hotspot detection, metric spatial calibration, and global one-to-one assignment of thermal hotspots to CTA perforators within a predefined periumbilical region of interest. The workflow was evaluated in 12 patients. Of 46 CTA perforators within the region of interest, 84.8% were successfully linked to thermographic hotspots, with a median spatial offset of 14.74 mm. Automated assignment excluded 76.1% of detected hotspots due to lack of anatomical correspondence, thereby reducing subjective interpretation. The proposed system enables quantitative multimodal validation of functional and anatomical imaging and provides objective support for perforator selection in clinical practice.

entries.title: HoloGene: Learning to Lift Sliced Spatial Transcriptomics to Holistic 3D Gene Fields
entries.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) provides spatially resolved gene expression measurements, but most 3D ST datasets are acquired as independently processed 2D sections. Computational approaches span slice registration and integration, explicit or generative interpolation, and coordinate-field modeling. Within the last family, implicit neural representations (INRs) offer a continuous, coordinate-queryable parameterization, but standard isotropic coordinate encodings do not explicitly reflect that serial-section measurements are dense in-plane and sparse along the axial direction. We present HoloGene, an anisotropic conditional INR framework for estimating continuous 3D gene-expression fields from pre-registered ST sections. Its central contribution is an acquisition-aware factorization that couples dense in-plane synthesis with sparse axial evolution using established GAE, FiLM, pseudo-label supervision, and CORAL components. HoloGene compresses high-dimensional expression profiles into a graph-autoencoder latent manifold, uses pseudo-label-derived signature conditioning to provide coarse intra-section context, and applies depth-dependent FiLM modulation to model axial variation. A signature-stratified correlation-alignment regularizer encourages cross-slice covariance alignment in latent features. Using held-out measured sections as cross-sectional references, HoloGene improves reconstruction accuracy and biological preservation metrics compared with general-purpose INRs and adapted spatial-transcriptomics baselines. These results support anisotropic conditional modeling as a practical strategy for estimating 3D expression fields from discontinuous ST sections. Code is available at https://github.com/Szym29/HoloGene.

entries.title: Beyond AUC: Do Mammography Risk Models Predict When Cancer Occurs?
entries.abstract: Longitudinal deep learning models for mammography-based breast cancer risk prediction output either per-year cumulative risks or a discrete distribution over the year of diagnosis, from which cumulative risks F1,...,F5 are derived. These models are evaluated almost exclusively with year-wise AUCs and the concordance index. We show that these metrics are largely insensitive to when cancer occurs: they can be high even for a model that carries no information about the year of diagnosis. We re-evaluate two recent longitudinal models (OA-BreaCR, LMV-Net) on CSAW-CC with a 5-year horizon using timing metrics computed on cancer cases only. Despite C-indices up to 0.75, neither orders cancer cases by time to diagnosis significantly better than chance (c_time 0.51 and 0.55, both 95% CIs covering 0.5). Weighted absolute timing error favours a constant "year 3" prediction over both models, so we use c_time as the primary timing metric. For Mirai's additive-hazard head, also used by LMV-Net, we analyse how per-year increments passed through a ReLU can collapse under severe class imbalance. We also propose a breast-level, two-stage model that separates whether from when. It matches LMV-Net in discrimination (C-index 0.745 vs. 0.746) but orders cancer cases better (c_time 0.58 vs. 0.51, paired 95% CI of the difference 0.01-0.13), on par with Mirai's published weights (0.57).
entries.comment: 7 pages, 2 figures, 1 table. Submitted to ISBI 2027

entries.title: Scaling large language model-assisted line-of-therapy adjudication with human-in-the-loop evidence-calibrated selection
entries.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have enabled the ability to scale clinical adjudication tasks traditionally dependent on exhaustive manual review. Line-of-therapy (LoT) adjudication, a major bottleneck in oncology cohort construction, is a prime example. Line boundaries must be inferred from longitudinal treatment histories according to nuanced, study-specific definitions, at every regimen transition for every patient. LLMs can apply this adjudication at scale, but their reliability varies across patients. Treatment histories differ in complexity, and ambiguous or atypical patterns depend on expert clinical judgment. Reliable automation thus requires verified support for model assignments and the ability to identify cases that warrant manual review. Here, we present evidence-calibrated selection (ECS), a human-in-the-loop framework for scaling LLM-assisted LoT adjudication. ECS derives confidence from observed clinician adjudications, prioritizes patients with the least-supported assignments for follow-up review, and returns completed adjudications to the model as precedent. As the evidence base grows, ECS continuously calibrates confidence to estimate residual error, thus enabling more efficient use of clinician time. In simulations on 136 clinician adjudicated patients with multiple myeloma, ECS achieved a residual error of 5% after review of 44.6% of patients, compared to 62.2% when review was directed by LLM self-reported confidence and 81.9% under random sampling. These results support a scalable approach to study-specific LoT adjudication, using clinician evidence to inform automated predictions, minimize error, and reduce review burden.

entries.title: Deep Sequence Model for Genome Wide Discovery of Coding and Regulatory Element Signatures
entries.abstract: Interpreting deep neural networks for genomic sequence classification remains challenging despite strong predictive performance. We develop a lightweight CNN with post-training gradient-based analysis to identify which sequence positions drive coding versus intergenomic classification. Applied to the standardized demo_coding_vs_intergenomic_seqs dataset, our model achieves 91.87% validation accuracy while revealing interpretable patterns: nine hot spots with consistently high importance, clear class-specific separation at positions 20-100 (coding) and 150-190 (intergenomic), and a strong mean-variance correlation (r = 0.530) indicating robust discriminative features. Gradient-based importance analysis shows that the model implicitly learns biologically meaningful sequence distinctions without explicit annotations. This work demonstrates that neural network interpretability and accuracy can coexist, providing a framework for understanding genomic sequence classification and enabling biology-driven hypothesis generation.
entries.comment: 4 pages, 3 figures, 1 table. Accepted at CVIS 2025. A shorter 3-page version was published in the Journal of Computational Vision and Imaging Systems, Vol. 11, No. 1 (2026)

entries.title: Automated Left Ventricle Strain Analysis from DENSE MRI
entries.abstract: Background: Quantifying myocardial strains from Displacement ENcoding with Stimulated Echoes (DENSE) MRI provides insight into left ventricular performance, but current data processing pipelines remain limited in automation, robustness, and full left ventricle coverage. Methods: We present a fully automated framework for voxel-wise displacement and strain analysis of the left ventricle from DENSE MRI. Our method integrates a multi-channel nnU-Net model trained on both magnitude and phase images for segmentation, an automated phase unwrapping approach, an adaptation of the regularized spatiotemporal least squares (RSTLS) formulation for displacement computation, and strain calculations based on radial basis function interpolation. The proposed framework enables the estimation of displacements and strains across the left ventricle from a full stack of short-axis images. Results: Validation using a computational phantom shows the framework's overall resilience to data noise. Following computational phantom evaluation, the proposed framework is applied to analyze DENSE MRI short-axis slices acquired in forty-seven (N=47) healthy volunteers and covering the full left ventricle. Circumferential, longitudinal, and radial strains are presented throughout the cardiac cycle and at peak systole, showcasing the performance of the proposed framework. Results show that circumferential and longitudinal strains are computed accurately. However, challenges persist when estimating radial strain, especially in the subendocardial layer. A group-wise strain comparison is also performed based on volunteers' sex and age showing a significant effect of sex on circumferential and longitudinal strains. Conclusions: Overall, the proposed framework provides an automated and modular pipeline to compute displacements and strains from DENSE MR images that can be scaled and generalized toward clinical applications.

entries.title: From the possible to the optimal: differentiable optimization of gene regulatory networks
entries.abstract: Understanding the space of ``the actual and the possible'' regulatory architectures capable of realizing biological functions is one of the major challenges in biology. Optimization-based approaches can rationalize regulatory mechanisms from functional objectives and constraints, but their computational cost has limited them to finding individual solutions. Here, we introduce \texttt{jaxgrn}, a framework that combines differentiable programming with stochastic simulations of gene regulatory networks (GRNs) to optimize thousands of networks end-to-end on GPUs. Using morphogen-driven embryonic patterning as a case study, we optimize networks for domain formation and positional information, while varying constraints on input noise, boundary precision and scaling with system size. While recovering known archetypes for scaling, we find that varying the constraints organizes optimal solutions into qualitatively distinct regimes. When optimizing domain formation, we observe phenotypic convergence across a continuum of regulatory architectures, ranging from input-driven to feedback-driven networks.
